newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Coffee pulls back but bullish tone intact.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Coffee pulls back but bullish tone intact.

text.p: Arabica coffee futures tumbled early Tuesday after the resolution of a state workers' strike in Colombia triggered a technical correction, but traders and anaylsts said bullish sentiment remained intact.
While prices may come under further pressure over the next few days, a strong fundamental outlook is likely to keep the market buoyant in the longer term, they said.
"In the near-term it is probably a turning point," said Prudential Securities analyst Arthur Stevenson. "But if we take a longer range perspective, I'm still a bull."
Stevenson said low stock levels in both consuming and producing countries would continue to underpin the market.
Dwindling coffee inventories are at the root of the sudden run-up on the futures market, which has seen coffee prices rocket some 50 percent since the beginning of the year.
"What we have is close to record low stocks," said Refco Inc analyst Ann Prendergast. "There is new coffee coming in but it is being absorbed by the market."

The Green Coffee Association of New York releases its January stock report after today's close, but while most analysts expect a modest increase from the 1.327 million 60-kg bags reported in December, they said it would probably not be a significant change.

Many analysts said the key to market's future is the size of next year's crop in top-producer Brazil. Reports that Brazil's 1997/98 harvest could come in significantly lower than the previous season's crop reignited supply jitters.
Preliminary forecasts by the Brazilian government have pegged the country's coming 1997/98 coffee crop between 18 million and 20 million bags compared with an estimated 25 million bags for 1996/97.

But talk former USDA representative and industry consultant Leon Yallouz said Brazil's coffee trees showed signs of recovery after two devastating frosts two years ago had traders speculating his unreleased estimate could come in well above government forecasts.

"The fundamentals are still bullish, but are they as bullish as last week? No way," said Smith Barney analyst Walter Spilka. "There is no more strike in Colombia and there have been comments the Brazilian crop may not be that bad."
Spilka added that high futures prices have coaxed producers to sell more coffee.
"High prices will bring more coffee into the market," he said. "And there is coffee out there."

Spilka said an agreement by Central American members of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) to juggle about 100,000 60-kg bags of January-June export quotas illustrated their desire to move out coffee.
"The ACPC basically got together to talk about how to get rid of coffee," he said.

Regional members said Tuesday morning that pressures from growers in certain countries, namely Costa Rica and El Salvador, had forced the bloc to tweak the export quota system. However, it was stressed the agreement did not mean export limits for the region would be exceeded.

ACPC nations have in place an export limit program through to June this year. In a recent ACPC full council gathering in Rio de Janeiro, member nations decided to cut January-December export limits this year by 1.3 million 60-kg bags.
Additionally, some analysts said further liquidation by speculators ahead of spot March's first notice day on Thursday could keep the pressure on.
